title: How do we know? Noticing, testing and asking 'Says who?'
source: DeepKids Combined, The Deep End: a DeepKids topic from the founder's Grade 1 concept grid (Fringe Science: wild ideas must be tested, not just imagined). No board teaches it at this class, so there are no board subtopics to cover. No textbook needed.
summary: Your child finds out that science is not a book of answers but a way of finding out: notice, wonder, make a guess you can test, test it fairly, repeat it, and tell others. They drop heavy and light things, test whether blowing on a die brings a six, grow a mould garden, and hear how mistakes and accidents opened doors (the mould that became penicillin). They meet Mary Anning, a poor girl whose fossils changed science while others took the credit, Alfred Wegener, whose 'wild' idea of moving continents was laughed at and turned out right, and C.V. Raman, who asked 'Says who?' of a famous scientist on a ship to England. They learn three questions to ask of every claim, including ours: Says who? How do they know? Who's missing?
builds_on: This is the first rung. It needs nothing earlier except a child who asks 'why?'. Class 3 adds fair tests with controls, 'a claim that can't be wrong can't be known right', extraordinary claims, cold fusion and plate tectonics, and the people left out of discovery stories. Class 5 adds blinding, replication, the difference between bold frontier science and fringe claims, and how science checks itself.
subconcepts: science is a way of finding out, not a list of answers
observation: noticing carefully with all the senses
a question and a guess you can test (hypothesis)
a fair test: change only one thing
evidence: what we can see, count or measure
repeat it: one try is not enough
changing your mind when the evidence changes
Says who? How do they know? Who's missing?
wild ideas must be tested: some win, most don't
mistakes and accidents that led to discoveries
who found it, and who got the credit
goals: By the end your child can say what scientists do: notice, wonder, guess, test, repeat and share.
By the end your child can turn a 'why?' into a guess they can test, and test it fairly by changing only one thing.
By the end your child can explain why one try is not enough, using their own dice results.
By the end your child can ask 'Says who? How do they know? Who's missing?' about a claim.
By the end your child can tell the story of Mary Anning or Alfred Wegener and say why people did not believe them at first.
By the end your child can sort statements into true, false and 'scientists disagree or don't know yet'.
words: a way of finding out how the world works by looking, testing and checking
to notice carefully, with eyes, ears, nose, hands and tongue
something you want to find out
something you do to see if your guess is right
a test where you change only one thing
what you see, count or measure that tells you if something is true
the remains or print of a living thing from long ago, turned to stone
finding out something nobody knew before
a fuzzy fungus that grows on old food
being thanked and named for something you did

days.title: Does the Moon follow you?
days.goal: Find out that we can check what we believe, starting with the Moon.

steps.title: How do you know?
steps.do: Ask three questions and, after each answer, ask 'How do you know?': 'Is it day or night now?' (I can see the sky is light.) 'Is the milk hot?' (I touched it, I saw steam.) 'Is there a Moon in the sky right now?' (Maybe I don't know; I'd have to look.) Say: 'Every time you said I saw, I touched, I heard, you were using evidence. Some things we know, some we guess, and some we don't know yet.' Write those three words on a big sheet: KNOW, GUESS, DON'T KNOW YET.

steps.title: Story: The Moon That Came Along
steps.do: Read the story aloud (Story tab). Then ask the story questions. Don't explain why the Moon seems to follow; ask: 'Ishaan thought the Moon was following only him. How did they find out it wasn't?' (They asked Aaji far away, and she saw it too.) 'What did the far mountain do that the near trees didn't?'

steps.title: Know, guess, don't know yet
steps.do: Say each sentence and your child points to KNOW, GUESS or DON'T KNOW YET on the sheet: 'The Sun will rise tomorrow' (know: it always has, and we know why). 'It will rain tomorrow' (guess). 'There are animals on other planets' (don't know yet: nobody knows!). 'Our cat loves us' (guess: how could we test it?). 'Ice melts in the sun' (know: we've seen it many times). Say: 'Scientists are people who move things from GUESS to KNOW by testing. And they are honest about DON'T KNOW YET.' Start a Wonder Wall: your child says three things they wonder about, and you write them on slips and stick them up (this is the start of the project).

need: sticky notes or paper slips and tape

days.title: Noticing, and a guess you can test
days.goal: Practise careful observation and turn a 'why' into a test.

steps.title: The ten-things walk
steps.do: Walk round the garden, terrace or lane for 10 minutes. Your child must notice ten things using at least four senses (the smell of wet soil, a bird call, rough bark, a line of ants). For each, ask 'What do you wonder about it?' and write one 'why' question. Say: 'This is what scientists do first: they notice. Most people walk past an ant line. A scientist stops.'

steps.title: Heavy and light: which lands first?
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. First ask: 'If I drop a heavy steel ball and a light plastic ball at the same time, which will land first?' Write your child's guess: that is a hypothesis, a guess you can test. Drop them together from the same height onto a cushion, five times. Your child watches and listens for two thuds or one. Then drop a flat sheet of paper and a crumpled one. Ask: 'Was your guess right? What's different about the flat paper?' (The air pushes on it.)

steps.title: Start the mould garden
steps.do: Set up Experiment e3: put a slice of bread, a piece of roti and a piece of orange peel, each lightly dampened, in three zip bags. Seal them and tape them shut. Ask: 'What do you think will happen in a week?' Draw them as they look today. Say: 'We'll come back to these. Some of the biggest discoveries started with old, mouldy things.'

need: a heavy steel ball or a stone and a light plastic ball of similar size
a slice of bread, a piece of roti, orange peel

days.title: Does blowing on the die bring a six?
days.goal: Learn the fair test and why one try is never enough.

steps.title: Lucky things
steps.do: Ask: 'Do you have a lucky thing? A lucky pencil, a lucky shirt?' Many people believe that blowing on a die before throwing brings a six. Ask: 'How could we find out if that's true?' Listen to their idea. Good answers: throw it lots of times with blowing and lots without, and count.

steps.title: The dice test
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Throw the die 20 times without blowing and 20 times with blowing, the same way each time, onto the same tray. Your child makes a tally mark for every six. Ask before you start: 'What must stay the same so the test is fair?' (Same die, same tray, same way of throwing. The only change is the blowing.) After 5 throws each, stop and ask: 'Can we decide now?' After 20 each, compare. Usually both get about three or four sixes, and the numbers wobble up and down.

steps.title: One try is not enough
steps.do: Ask: 'If your cousin blew on the die once and got a six, would that prove blowing works?' (No: you can get a six by chance. You need many throws.) 'If our test showed no difference, should we tell the cousin they're wrong?' (We can say what our evidence shows, and invite them to test it too.) Write on the big sheet: FAIR TEST = change only one thing. REPEAT IT = one try is not enough. Add to the Wonder Wall any new questions.

days.title: Happy accidents
days.goal: See how mistakes and accidents, noticed carefully, became discoveries.

steps.title: Mould garden check
steps.do: Look at the three sealed bags from Experiment e3 without opening them. Your child draws what they see: fuzzy patches? What colours? Which food has the most? Ask: 'Where did the mould come from? We didn't put any in.' (Tiny mould spores float in the air all the time, too small to see. They landed on the food before we sealed it.)

steps.title: The mould that saved lives
steps.do: Tell this true story: 'In 1928 a scientist in London, Alexander Fleming, came back from a holiday to his messy lab. He had left out little glass dishes of germs (bacteria). One dish had a blue-green mould on it, a mistake. Most people would have thrown it away. But Fleming noticed something odd: around the mould, the germs had died. He wondered why. That mould made a juice that kills germs, and it became the first antibiotic medicine, penicillin.' Then add: 'Fleming couldn't turn it into a medicine. Years later, a team in Oxford did it, with a lab helper called Norman Heatley who built the machines out of milk churns and bedpans. Who do you think should get the credit?' Ask: 'What was the mistake? What turned the mistake into a discovery?' (Noticing, and asking why.)

steps.title: Oops paintings
steps.do: Do Activity a1: each of you drops a blob of paint on paper, folds it, opens it, and turns the accidental blob into something (a butterfly, a monster, a map). Say: 'An accident only becomes a discovery when someone notices it and asks a question.' Your child tells you what they noticed in their blot.

days.title: The girl who found dragons
days.goal: Hear how a poor girl's evidence changed science, and who got the credit.

steps.title: Mary Anning
steps.do: Talk about voice v1. Tell it as a story: 'Mary Anning was born in 1799 in a seaside town in England called Lyme Regis. Her family was poor. She and her brother Joseph searched the crumbling cliffs for stone shells and bones to sell to tourists. When she was about 12, they dug out a whole skeleton of a giant sea creature with a long snout and huge eyes, an ichthyosaur (say ik-thee-oh-sor). People thought it was a crocodile. It wasn't: it was an animal that no longer lives anywhere. That was evidence that some kinds of animals die out for ever.' Ask the voice question. Then: 'Rich gentlemen bought her fossils and wrote about them, often without her name. She wasn't allowed to join their science club because she was a woman.' Ask: 'Who's missing from the story when only their names are written down?'

steps.title: Make a fossil
steps.do: Press a shell, a leaf or a toy dinosaur's foot into a flat ball of atta dough or clay, lift it out, and leave the print to dry. Say: 'A fossil is often just a print like this, or bones that slowly turned to stone, kept for millions of years in mud that became rock. Mary Anning learned to read them.' Ask: 'If someone finds your fossil in a million years, what could they tell about the thing that made it? What couldn't they tell?' (Its shape and size; not its colour, its sound, whether it was kind.)

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Your child does Worksheet ws1 (core). Read each item aloud. For the 'why' items, they say the answer and you write it. For every answer ask: 'How do you know?'

need: a handful of atta dough or clay

days.title: Wild ideas and 'Says who?'
days.goal: Meet wild ideas that won, see that famous people can be wrong, and play True, False or Scientists Disagree.

steps.title: The map puzzle
steps.do: Do Activity a2: cut out South America and Africa from a printed world map and slide them together. Ask: 'What do you notice?' (They fit like jigsaw pieces.) 'If they fitted together long ago, what must have happened?' Let your child guess before you tell them anything.

steps.title: Alfred Wegener's wild idea
steps.do: Talk about voice v3, Alfred Wegener, and ask its question. Say: 'He had a wild idea. Wild ideas are welcome in science, but they must be tested. His was tested for 50 years, and it won. Most wild ideas don't.' Ask: 'What else could explain why the coasts fit?' (Coincidence, which is why he also looked for matching fossils and rocks.)

steps.title: Why is the sea blue? Says who?
steps.do: Talk about voice v2, C.V. Raman on the ship. Ask: 'A very famous scientist said the sea is blue because it reflects the sky. Raman didn't just believe it. What did he do?' (He tested it: he blocked the sky's reflection and the sea was still blue.) Teach the three questions with a hand sign for each: 'Says who?' (point outward), 'How do they know?' (tap your eyes), 'Who's missing?' (open your hands). Say: 'Ask them of everyone. Of teachers. Of books. Of me.'

steps.title: True, False or Scientists Disagree?
steps.do: Play the card game (g1). Each player takes a card, reads it (or you read it), and puts it on TRUE, FALSE or SCIENTISTS DISAGREE / NOBODY KNOWS. Before turning it over they must say how they know or how someone could find out. Turn it over. Talk about the surprises: dinosaurs aren't all gone (birds are dinosaurs), and whether trees talk is still argued about.

prep.task: Print a world map and the True/False cards; cut the cards out

days.title: I can find out
days.goal: Review, finish the Wonder Wall project and teach it back.

steps.title: Mould garden: last look
steps.do: Look at the sealed bags one last time (Experiment e3). Ask: 'Which food grew the most mould? Was your guess from Day 2 right? What would you change to make it a fair test?' (Same size pieces, all equally wet, same place.) Then throw the bags away still sealed.

steps.title: Stretch and challenge
steps.do: Your child does Worksheet ws2 (stretch), and, if they are keen, two or three items from Worksheet ws3 (challenge), with you reading aloud. On the challenge 'what if' items, take any well-reasoned answer.

steps.title: Test one wonder
steps.do: Do the last part of the project: your child picks one question from the Wonder Wall that you can test at home (for example 'Do ants like sugar more than salt?' or 'Which paper boat floats longest?'). Together, write: My question, My guess, How I'll test it fairly, What happened. Do the test now if it is quick. Look at Worksheet ws3 together for one of its puzzles if there's time.

steps.title: Check and teach it back
steps.do: Ask the check questions aloud. Then your child teaches it back: they explain to another family member what scientists do (notice, wonder, guess, test, repeat, share), using the dice test as an example, and ask them the three questions: 'Says who? How do they know? Who's missing?'

often the person with more power, money or fame

sections.p: What if nobody was ever allowed to say 'I was wrong'? What would happen to science?
Your Nani says the crows cawing means guests are coming. How could you test it? What would you count?
Ask 'Who's missing?' about the penicillin story. Who helped that we usually forget?

experiments.title: Heavy and light: which lands first?
experiments.question: Do heavy things fall faster than light things?
need: a heavy ball (steel, or a smooth stone) and a light ball of about the same size
steps: Your child writes or says their guess.
Stand on the floor (not a chair) and hold both balls at the same height, about as high as your shoulders.
Let go at exactly the same moment over the cushion. Listen: one thud or two?
Repeat five times, taking turns to drop and to watch.
Now drop a flat sheet of paper and a crumpled sheet of paper together.
Drop a flat sheet and a heavy book together, then put the flat sheet on top of the book and drop them.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which will land first, the heavy ball or the light ball? How much sooner?'
experiments.observe: The two balls land at almost the same moment. The crumpled paper falls much faster than the flat sheet. A sheet resting on top of a book falls with the book.
experiments.why: Gravity pulls on heavy things more, but heavy things are also harder to get moving, and the two effects cancel out, so without air everything falls at the same speed. Air pushes back on falling things (air resistance). It hardly matters for balls, but a flat sheet of paper catches a lot of air and floats down. On top of the book, the book pushes the air away. In 1971 an astronaut on the Moon, where there is no air, dropped a hammer and a feather together and they landed at the same time.
experiments.safety: Drop from standing height onto a cushion, away from toes and glass. Don't climb on furniture.

experiments.title: The lucky-blow dice test
experiments.question: Does blowing on a die make a six more likely?
steps: Agree the rules: same die, same tray, shake in cupped hands and throw the same way every time.
Throw 20 times without blowing. Make a tally mark every time a six comes up.
Throw 20 times, blowing on the die in your hands before each throw. Tally the sixes.
After the first 5 throws of each, stop and compare. Then carry on to 20.
Compare the totals. If you have time, do 20 more of each and add them up.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will blowing give us more sixes? How many sixes do you expect out of 20 throws?'
experiments.observe: Both ways usually give about three or four sixes in 20 throws, but it wobbles: sometimes one, sometimes six. After only 5 throws the results can look very different; after 40 they get closer.
experiments.why: A fair die has six faces, so each face comes up about one time in every six throws, whatever you do before throwing. Small numbers of throws can look 'lucky' just by chance, which is why scientists repeat tests many times before deciding. Testing a belief fairly, instead of arguing about it, is the heart of science.

experiments.title: The sealed mould garden
experiments.question: Where does mould grow, and where does it come from?
need: a slice of bread, a piece of roti, a piece of orange peel
steps: Sprinkle a few drops of water on each food.
Put each in its own zip bag, seal it, and tape the seal shut.
Label the bags and leave them in a warm, dark cupboard.
Draw the food on Day 2, Day 4 and Day 7. Never open the bags.
On Day 7, throw the bags in the bin still sealed.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will anything grow? Which food will grow the most?'
experiments.observe: Fuzzy patches of white, green, blue-green or black mould appear, usually first on the bread. They spread and change colour.
experiments.why: Moulds are fungi. Their spores, far too small to see, float in the air everywhere and land on food. With water, warmth and food, they grow into the fuzzy threads you see. One blue-green mould, Penicillium, makes a chemical that kills some bacteria: Alexander Fleming noticed this in 1928, and it became the medicine penicillin.
experiments.safety: Never open the bags or sniff the mould: the spores can make people ill, especially anyone with asthma or allergies. Throw them away sealed. Wash hands after handling.
experiments.time: 8 min, then 3 short checks over 5 days

activities.title: Oops paintings
steps: Drop a blob or two of paint in the middle of a sheet.
Fold the paper in half, press, and open it.
Look at the accidental shape. What does it remind you of?
Add eyes, legs, words or colour to turn it into something.
Give it a name and say one thing you noticed that you didn't plan.
activities.outcome: A painting made from an accident, and the idea that noticing turns an accident into a discovery.

activities.title: The continent jigsaw
steps: Find South America and Africa on the map.
Cut them out along the coast.
Slide them across the paper towards each other. Do they fit?
Look for other pieces that might fit.
Ask: 'If they fitted together long ago, what must have happened?'
activities.outcome: A map puzzle showing the clue that made Alfred Wegener think the continents had moved.

voices.idea: A poor, self-taught fossil hunter from Lyme Regis. With her brother Joseph she uncovered the first ichthyosaur skeleton to be recognised (about 1811–1812), and later the first nearly complete plesiosaur (1823). Her finds were key evidence that some kinds of animals had gone extinct, and that Earth's past was very long.
voices.then: Rich collectors and scientists bought her fossils and wrote about them, often without naming her. As a woman she could not join the Geological Society of London. When she found the plesiosaur, the famous French scientist Georges Cuvier at first thought it might be a fake, because its neck was so long; when he looked closely, he agreed it was real.
voices.now: She is now remembered as one of the great fossil hunters. In 2010 the Royal Society named her among the most influential British women in science, and in 2022 a statue of her was put up in Lyme Regis after a campaign started by a schoolgirl.
voices.ask: Cuvier thought the plesiosaur might be fake. What should he do before deciding: trust his feeling, trust Mary, or look at the bones?

voices.idea: In 1921, on a ship to England, Raman looked at the deep blue Mediterranean Sea. The famous scientist Lord Rayleigh had said the sea is blue mainly because it reflects the blue sky. Raman used a small prism that blocks reflected light, looked at the water, and it was still blue. He decided that water itself scatters light and makes the blue.
voices.then: He published his idea in 1921. It led him and his student K.S. Krishnan to a new discovery about how light scatters, the Raman effect, in 1928.
voices.now: Scientists agree that the sea's blue comes mostly from the water itself, which soaks up red light, and partly from scattering and the sky's reflection. Raman won the Nobel Prize in 1930. Krishnan, who did much of the work with him, was not included.
voices.ask: Raman checked an idea from a very famous scientist. Is it rude to test what a famous person says? Why or why not?

voices.idea: In 1912 Wegener said the continents were once joined in one giant land and have slowly drifted apart. His evidence: the coasts of Africa and South America fit, the same fossils and rocks are found on both sides of the ocean, and coal is found in icy Antarctica.
voices.then: Most geologists laughed. He could not explain what force could push whole continents, and he was a weather scientist, not a geologist.
voices.now: In the 1950s and 1960s, maps of the ocean floor (made with the help of Marie Tharp) and other evidence showed that the Earth's crust is made of plates that move a few centimetres a year. Wegener was mostly right. He died on an expedition in Greenland in 1930, before he was believed.
voices.ask: Wegener had good clues but no explanation of how. Were the other scientists wrong to doubt him? What would have convinced you?

check.q: What do scientists do to find out about the world?
check.a: They notice, wonder (ask a question), make a guess they can test, test it fairly, repeat it, and share it so others can check.
A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same.

check.q: Why isn't one throw of a die enough to know if blowing on it works?
check.a: You can get a six by chance. You have to throw it many times each way and compare.

check.q: What are the three questions to ask about any claim?
check.a: Says who? How do they know? Who's missing?

check.q: How did a messy mistake help Alexander Fleming?
check.a: Mould grew on his dish by accident; he noticed the germs around it had died, asked why, and found penicillin.

check.q: Who was Mary Anning and why do we tell her story?
check.a: A poor girl in England who found giant fossils that showed some animals had died out for ever; others often took the credit and she was not allowed into the science club.

check.q: Should we believe every wild idea? What should we do?
check.a: No: we should test it. Some wild ideas, like Wegener's moving continents, turn out right; most turn out wrong.

project.title: The Wonder Wall
steps: On Day 1, start a Wonder Wall on a door or wall: every question your child wonders about goes on a slip.
Each day, add at least one new question from the walk, the tests or the stories.
Sort the slips into three groups: 'I can test it at home', 'I need to ask or read', and 'Nobody knows yet'.
On Day 7, pick one testable question. Write: My question, My guess, How I'll test it fairly, What happened.
Do the test and add the result to the wall, with a drawing.
Keep the wall going after this week: when a question is answered, ask 'How do we know?'
project.outcome: A wall of your child's own questions, sorted by how they could be answered, and one real fair test they designed and ran themselves.

game.title: True, False or Scientists Disagree?
rules: Put the three category cards face up in a row: TRUE, FALSE and SCIENTISTS DISAGREE / NOBODY KNOWS. Shuffle the other cards face down.
On your turn, take the top card and read it (a grown-up can read for younger players).
Put it under the category you think is right, and say how you know, or how someone could find out.
Turn it over. If you are right, keep it. If not, put it at the bottom of the pile.
If you gave a good 'how could we find out' even when wrong, you may keep it anyway, if the other players agree.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most cards wins. Then pick the most surprising card and talk about it.

big: How can you know something for sure? Is there anything you are completely sure of?
Is it brave or silly to believe a wild idea before anyone has tested it?
Your dog knows the world by smell, a bat by echoes. Are their kinds of knowing as good as ours?
If someone finds out something new but nobody writes their name down, did they still discover it?
Is it all right to say 'I don't know'? Who is braver: someone who says it, or someone who pretends?

challenge.q: Galileo is said to have dropped two balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa to show heavy and light things fall together. Did he?
challenge.hint: The story was told by his student Vincenzo Viviani many years later, and Galileo never described doing it, so many historians doubt it happened that way. A Dutch scientist, Simon Stevin, did report dropping two lead balls from a church tower in Delft in 1586, and they landed together. Galileo did real experiments with balls rolling down slopes. Ask: why might one famous name collect all the stories?

challenge.q: Many people say Columbus proved the Earth was round. Is that right?
challenge.hint: No. Educated people had known the Earth is round for about 2,000 years before Columbus. The Greek scholar Eratosthenes measured its size around 240 BCE using shadows, and in India Aryabhata wrote in 499 CE that the Earth spins. The argument with Columbus was about how big the Earth was, and he was wrong about that. Ask: how could you show a friend that the Earth is round, without a rocket?

challenge.q: Fleming discovered penicillin all by himself. True?
challenge.hint: Fleming noticed the mould in 1928, but he could not make enough of it to use as a medicine. In Oxford, Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and the lab helper Norman Heatley made it work about 12 years later, and a lab worker in America, Mary Hunt, found a mouldy melon at a market that grew much more of it. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize; Heatley and Hunt did not. Ask: who else should be in the story?

perspectives.who: A farmer in a Maharashtra village
perspectives.view: Many farmers say that when ants carry their eggs to higher ground, rain is coming. This is knowledge built from watching for years, though it is rarely written down. Ask: how could we test it? Who should get credit if it turns out true?

A dog finds out about the world mainly through its nose: who walked by, what they ate, how they felt. It 'knows' things we can't. Ask: is smelling a kind of evidence? What do we miss because we use mostly our eyes?

A detective doesn't just believe what people say. They look for clues, check stories against each other, and change their mind when a new clue turns up. Ask: how is a scientist like a detective? How is it different?
Babies drop spoons again and again and watch them fall. Some scientists say babies are little scientists, testing the world. Ask: what were you testing when you were a baby?

story.title: The Moon That Came Along
text: The night bus from Pune to Kolhapur smelled of oranges, diesel and somebody's jasmine. Ishaan had the window seat because he was six and his sister Tara was nine, and Amma said that was the rule, though Tara said it was a rule that had been invented on the spot.
The bus roared out of the city, past the last petrol pump and the last chai stall, and the dark came up on both sides. Then Ishaan saw it. A huge, round, white Moon, sitting just above the hills.

He watched it for a long time. The bus went round a bend. The Moon came too. The bus climbed a slope. The Moon climbed with it. The bus stopped at a red light in a small town where one dog was asleep in the road, and the Moon stopped, and waited.
'Tara,' he whispered. 'The Moon is following me.'
Tara did not look up from her book. 'It's following me,' she said. 'I'm older.'
'It's following me. It stopped when we stopped. I saw.'
'You can't both be right,' said Amma sleepily from the seat in front. 'Unless you are.'
This was the kind of thing Amma said, and it was very annoying.

Ishaan pressed his nose to the glass. The trees beside the road rushed past, whoosh, whoosh, whoosh, gone before he could count them. The electric poles flicked by like the ticks of a clock. But far away, a long dark mountain with one light on top did not rush. It slid along slowly, almost keeping up with the bus. And the Moon did not move at all. It just came along.
Tara had put her book down. She was watching too.
'Here's a test,' she said, because she had just learned about tests at school and she said it a lot now. 'If the Moon is following you, then when you close your eyes it won't know where you are.'
Ishaan closed his eyes and counted to twenty. When he opened them, the Moon was right there, exactly where it had been, as if it had been politely waiting.
'That proves it,' he said. 'It likes me.'
'That proves nothing,' said Tara. 'Let's do another test.' She took Amma's phone, which she was not supposed to do, and called Aaji.
Aaji lived in Nagpur, which was very, very far, a whole night's train away in the other direction. She answered on the second ring, because she never slept before eleven.
'Aaji,' said Tara. 'Go outside and look at the sky. Is there a Moon?'
They heard the creak of Aaji's terrace door and the slap of her chappals on the steps and the far-off sound of somebody's television. Then Aaji's voice came back, soft with wonder.
'Oh,' she said. 'Yes. It's big tonight. Round and white, just over the water tank. I'm sitting on my chair and it is sitting with me.'
Ishaan stared at the Moon outside the bus window. Then he stared at the phone.
'But it's here,' he said. 'It's with me.'
'It's with me too,' said Aaji.
Nobody said anything for a while. The bus hummed. The trees went whoosh, whoosh. The far mountain slid slowly. The Moon did not move at all.
Ishaan thought about the trees, which were close, and rushed. And the mountain, which was far, and slid. And the Moon, which did not move even a little.
'Tara,' he said slowly. 'What if the things that are close go fast, and the things that are far go slow, and the Moon is so far away that it doesn't go at all?'
Tara opened her mouth to say something clever, and closed it again.
'So far,' said Ishaan, 'that it can be with me, and with Aaji, and with that dog in the road, all at the same time.'
'That's a hypothesis,' said Tara at last. 'That's a guess you can test.' But she said it in a different voice, a quieter one, not the voice for winning.

For a moment Ishaan felt a little sad. He had liked the Moon being his. It had felt like a secret friend. Then he looked at the phone, where Aaji's face was a small bright square, her silver hair lit up by the very same light that was coming through the bus window and landing on his hands.
'Aaji,' he said. 'Can you see it now?'
'I can see it.'
'I'm looking at it too,' he said. 'So we're looking at the same thing.'
'We are,' said Aaji.

They stayed on the phone a long time, not talking much, an old woman on a terrace in Nagpur and a small boy on a bus near Satara and his sister, who had given up being older for one night, all three of them looking up.
The Moon came along, all the way to Kolhapur, and all the way to everywhere.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the story turns twice. First, Ishaan's belief is tested with someone else's evidence: Aaji, far away, sees the Moon 'following' her too, so it cannot be following only him. Then he notices that near things rush past and far things slide slowly, and guesses that the Moon is so far away it doesn't seem to move at all. That is a real explanation (it is called parallax), reached by noticing and guessing, and it is a hypothesis he could test. The loss of the Moon as 'his' becomes something shared: the same light on everyone.
ask: Ishaan thought the Moon was following only him. What evidence changed his mind?
Why did the trees rush past but the mountain slide slowly?
Tara said 'That's a hypothesis.' What was the guess, and how could you test it on your next car or bus ride?
How did Ishaan feel when he found out the Moon wasn't only his? Did the feeling change?
Who else in the whole world might have been looking at the same Moon that night?

ideas.idea: Science is a way of finding out, not a book of answers.
ideas.more: Anyone can do it: notice, wonder, guess, test, repeat and share. Show it with the dice test, where your child's own tally marks decide the answer, not a grown-up.

ideas.idea: Evidence beats 'because I said so', even from famous people.
ideas.more: Raman tested Lord Rayleigh's idea; Mary Anning's bones beat the experts' doubts. Teach the three questions with hand signs: Says who? How do they know? Who's missing? And invite your child to ask them of you.

ideas.idea: Mistakes and wild ideas can be doors, if someone notices and tests them.
ideas.more: Fleming's messy dish became penicillin; Wegener's 'silly' idea became plate tectonics. But most wild ideas turn out wrong, so they must be tested, not just believed.

ideas.idea: The story of a discovery is also a story of who was left out.
ideas.more: Mary Anning, Norman Heatley and K.S. Krishnan did real work and were often not named. Whenever you hear a discovery story, ask who else was there.

unknowns: How many kinds of living things share the Earth with us? Scientists have named about two million, but there may be many millions more that nobody has ever described.
Is there life anywhere else in the universe? Nobody knows yet, and scientists are looking.
Why do we dream, and do animals dream like us? Scientists have ideas but no one is sure.

books.author: Laurence Anholt

books.author: Andrea Beaty
books.why: A girl who never stops asking 'why?' and tests everything, which is exactly this week.

books.author: Andrea Beaty
books.why: A girl whose flying machine crashes, and whose great-aunt cheers the failure. A good one for the day on mistakes.
